Ἀβραὰμ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. ἐπὶ τίνι ἐπίστευσεν Ἀβραὰμ τῷ
θεῷ οὐ πάνυ σαφῶς διηγήσατο ἡ γραφή· ἔοικεν δὲ ὁ ἀπόστολος καθόλου αὐτὸν
ἐκλαμβάνειν πεπιστευκέναι. καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῶς, εἰ μὲν τὸ καθόλου, πάντως καὶ τὸ κατὰ
μέρος· εἰ δ' ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰρημένοις ἐπίστευσεν τῷ θεῷ, οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ ὅτι καθόλου
ἐπίστευσεν· ἔστιν γὰρ μέτρα τοῦ πιστεύειν θεῷ· διὸ Ἀβραὰμ μὲν ἐπίστευσε τῷ θεῷ
καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, οὐδὲν δὲ τοιοῦτον γέγραπται ἡνίκα εἶδεν Ἰ ραὴλ
τὴν χεῖρα τὴν μεγάλην ἃ ἐποίη ε κύριο τοῖ Αἰγυπτίοι · καὶ ἐφοβήθη ὁ λαὸ τὸν
κύριον· καὶ ἐπί τευ ε τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ Μω ῇ τῷ θεράποντι αὐτοῦ, οὐ πρόσκειται δὲ ὡς
ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ τὸ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. νομίζω δὲ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν
μὴ ἐπιστήσαντας τῇ ἀκριβείᾳ τῆς γραφῆς ἐκτεθήσεσθαι τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς Γενέσεως ῥητὸν
οὐχ ὡς Παῦλος αὐτὸ ἔθηκεν ἐν τῇ ἀρχῇ· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ ὁ οὕτως ἀκριβὴς ἐξέθετο τὸ
ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην, ἀλλ' ἐπίστευσεν
δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ θεῷ. οὕτω δὲ εἰκὸς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς γεγράφθαι ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους
ἐπιστολῇ ὅτι ἐλογί θη ἡ πί τι τῷ Ἀβραὰμ εἰ δικαιο ύνην. νυνὶ δὲ ἔχομεν ἡμεῖς
Ἀβραάμ. 22 iv 4, 5 τῷ δὲ ἐργαζομένῳ ὁ μισθὸς οὐ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ
ὀφείλημα· τῷ δὲ μὴ ἐργαζομένῳ, πιστεύοντι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἀσεβῆ,
λογίζεται ἡ πίστις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην. οὐδὲν ὧν δίδωσιν ὁ θεὸς τῇ γενητῇ φύσει
ὡς ὀφείλων δίδωσιν, ἀλλὰ πάντα ὡς χάριν δωρεῖται· καὶ πάντα τὰ εὐεργετούμενα
οὐκ ὀφειλομένης αὐτοῖς εὐεργεσίας εὐεργετεῖται, ἀλλὰ τῷ βούλεσθαι τὸν θεὸν ἰδίᾳ
χάριτι εὐεργετεῖν οὓς ἂν εὐεργετῇ. νῦν οὖν νομιστέον αὐτὸ ἁπλούστερον καὶ
καθόλου εἰρῆσθαι καὶ ἄλλως κοινότερον νοούμενον ἐπὶ τῶν οἱστισινοῦν
ἐργαζομένων καὶ τὸν μισθὸν ἀπ' ἐκείνων λαμβανόντων, οὐ κατὰ χάριν ἀλλὰ κατὰ
ὀφείλημα. ἡγητέον δὲ αὐτὸ δύνασθαι λέγεσθαι φέρε εἰπεῖν ἐπὶ τῶν ὡς Κάιν ἐργαζο
μένων τὴν γῆν καὶ ποιούντων ἔργα πονηρά· τούτοις γὰρ ὡς ὀφειλόμενα νομίζω καὶ
ὡς μισθὸν τῶν ἡμαρτημένων ἀποδίδοσθαι τὰς κολάσεις. διὸ καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος
ὀψώνια μὲν τῆ ἁμαρτία ἔφησεν εἶναι τὸν θάνατον· οὐκέτι δὲ ὀψώνια καὶ ὡσπερεὶ
ὀφειλόμενα ἀπὸ θεοῦ τὴν αἰώνιον ζωήν, ἀλλὰ χάρι μα αὐτοῦ· φησὶ γὰρ τὸ χάρι μα
τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιο ἐν Χρι τῷ Ἰη οῦ τῷ κρίῳ ἡμῶν. οὐ νομιστέον οὖν ἐπὶ τῶν
κρειττόνων ἔργων λέγεσθαι ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τὸ ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε ἀντιμετρηθή εται
ὑμῖν· χάριτι γάρ ἐ μεν ε ω μένοι· καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐξ ἡμῶν, θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον, ἵνα μή τι
καυχή ηται. πρὸς δὲ μέτρον τῶν ἡμαρτημένων ἡμῖν δίδοσθαι τὰς κολάσεις
ὑποληπτέον. 23 iv 6–9 καθάπερ καὶ ∆αυεὶδ λέγει τὸν μακαρισμὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ᾧ ὁ
θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων· μακάριοι ὧν ἀφέθησαν αἱ ἀνομίαι, καὶ ὧν
ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι· μακάριος ἀνὴρ ᾧ οὐ μὴ λογίσηται κύριος ἁμαρτίαν· ὁ
μακαρισμὸς οὖν οὗτος, ἐπὶ τὴν περιτομὴν ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν; μηκέτι
πραττομένου τοῦ χείρονος ἄφεσις εἰκὸς δύναται γενέσθαι ἀνομιῶν· ἀγαθοῦ δ'
ἐπιτελουμένου, ὡς τὰ γενόμενα κώλυμα γενέσθαι τῶν προημαρτημένων
ἐξαφανίζοντα αὐτῶν τὴν φύσιν, ἐπικαλύπτονται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι· ὧν προαγόντων, οὐδὲ
λογίζεται ἔτι κύριός τινι τὸ ἡμαρτηκέναι. 24 iv 9–12 λέγομεν γὰρ ὅτι ἐλογίσθη τῷ
Ἀβραὰμ ἡ πίστις εἰς δικαιοσύνην· πῶς οὖν ἐλογίσθη; ἐν περιτομῇ ὄντι, ἢ ἐν
ἀκροβυστίᾳ; οὐκ ἐν περιτομῇ ἀλλ' ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ· καὶ σημεῖον ἔλαβεν περιτομῆς,
σφραγῖδα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν
πατέρα πάντων τῶν πιστευόν των δι' ἀκροβυστίας, εἰς τὸ λογισθῆναι καὶ αὐτοῖς τὴν
δικαιοσύνην· καὶ πατέρα περιτομῆς τοῖς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς
στοιχοῦσι τοῖς ἴχνεσι τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀβραάμ.
λαμβάνει δὲ μετὰ τὴν ἐκ πίστεως δικαίωσιν σημεῖον περιτομῆς ὡσπερεὶ σφραγῖδα
pass_a_gloss: Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. The Scripture does not clearly state in what Abraham believed God; the apostle seems to take it generally that he had believed. For if it is universal, then it is also particular; but if he believed God regarding the things said, it does not follow that he believed universally, for there are measures of believing God. Thus Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, yet nothing of this sort is written when Israel saw the great hand which the Lord did against the Egyptians, and the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in Moses his servant; no such crediting is applied as in Abraham's case. I think those from the nations who have not been attentive to the accuracy of Scripture will be set forth the explicit statement from Genesis not as Paul placed it at the beginning; for such a precise person would not have set forth the belief of Abraham in God and its crediting as righteousness, but only that Abraham believed in God. So it is likely also written in the following in the Epistle to the Romans that the crediting was of faith to Abraham for righteousness. Now we have Abraham. To the one who works, the wage is not credited as grace but as debt; but to the one who does not work, yet believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness. Nothing that God gives to human nature as owed is given as owed, but all is given as grace; and all the good deeds done are not done as owed beneficence, but are done by God's will to show grace to whomever He does good. Now we must consider this simply and universally stated, and more commonly understood regarding those who work for wages and receive them not as grace but as debt. It must be considered that this can be said of those like Cain who work the earth and do evil works; for I consider these things as owed and as wages to be paid to the sinners. Therefore the apostle said that the wages of sin are death, but no longer are wages and as it were owed things from God eternal life, but grace of His; for He says that the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. We must not consider that in the gospel the measure by which you measure will be measured back to you is spoken of concerning excellent works; for by grace we remain; and this is not from us, but the gift of God, lest anyone should boast. Regarding the measure of our sins, the punishments must be considered as given to us.
pass_b_english: Abraham placed his trust in God, and that trust was counted as righteousness. The text does not specify exactly what he believed about God, though the apostle seems to treat it as a general conviction. If belief were truly universal, then it would necessarily include every particular; but if Abraham only believed God concerning the specific promises made to him, it does not follow that his belief was all-encompassing, for there are degrees and measures in how one trusts God. Thus, while Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness, no such reckoning is recorded when Israel witnessed the mighty acts of the Lord against Egypt, feared the Lord, and believed in Him and in Moses His servant. I suspect those from the nations who have not been careful in reading Scripture will now be presented with the explicit statement from Genesis—not as Paul placed it at the outset—but only as a bare acknowledgment that Abraham believed in God. Such a precise writer would not have framed Abraham’s belief and its reward as righteousness unless he meant to emphasize the gift nature of that credit. It is therefore likely that in the Epistle to the Romans, the apostle intends to show that it was faith—specifically Abraham’s faith—that was credited to him for righteousness. Now we turn to Abraham himself. To the one who labors, the wage is not regarded as a gift but as a debt owed; but to the one who does not work, yet trusts in the One who justifies the ungodly, that faith is counted as righteousness. Nothing that God gives to human nature as due is actually given as an obligation; rather, all is bestowed as grace. Even the good deeds performed are not done out of a sense of owed beneficence, but flow from God’s will to extend grace to whomever He chooses to bless. We must grasp this simply and universally: it applies clearly to those who work for wages and receive them not as grace but as what is due. This too can be said of those like Cain, who till the soil and do evil works—for I regard such actions as owed, as wages to be paid to sinners. Hence the apostle declares that the wages of sin are death, but no longer are the wages of God seen as owed things like eternal life; instead, eternal life is given as His grace. For He says that the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. We must not suppose that in the gospel, the principle by which you measure will be measured back to you refers to excellent works; for we stand by grace, and this is not from us, but the gift of God, so that no one may boast. Regarding the measure of our sins, the punishments must be understood as given to us.

Furthermore, just as David speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God credits righteousness apart from works—blessed are those whose lawlessness is forgiven, whose sins are covered, blessed is the one against whom the Lord will not count sin—this blessedness, then, is it tied to circumcision or to uncircumcision? We say that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness—but how? Was it while he was circumcised, or while he was uncircumcised? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision; and he received the sign of circumcision as a seal, a seal of the righteousness that comes by faith in the uncircumcised state, so that he might be the father of all who believe without circumcision, and that righteousness might be credited to them as well. And he is father not only of the circumcised, but also of those who walk in the steps of the faith that our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised. He receives, after being justified by faith, the sign of circumcision as it were a seal.

choices.issue: universality vs. particularity of Abraham's faith
choices.choice: Abraham's belief in God was particular to the promises made to him, not a universal trust in all things, and thus his faith's credit as righteousness reflects a specific, measured trust rather than an all-encompassing conviction.

choices.issue: basis of God's giving to humanity
choices.choice: All that God gives to human nature is given as grace, not as debt or owed obligation, and even good works flow from His will to show grace, not from any sense of earned merit.
